claims.text: An ML-augmented interatomic potential can accurately reproduce solid- and liquid-phase free energies in multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The predicted free energies can retain contributions from vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The ML-assisted method can reduce computational cost by an order of magnitude relative to explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD.
The ML potential will be trained on representative ab initio free-energy landscapes and selected molecular-dynamics snapshots from both solid and liquid phases.
Thermodynamic integration will be coupled to the ML potential to evaluate phase free energies.
The proposed domain includes elemental systems, binary systems, and high-entropy systems containing 4–8 components near and above their melting points.
Ab initio molecular dynamics is computationally prohibitive for the specified 4–8-component high-entropy systems.
Strategic sampling of ab initio configurations can provide a faithful representation of local atomic environments and phase-specific features.
Strategically sampled configurations can capture anharmonic effects.
Strategically sampled configurations can capture electron–vibration effects.
The ML model interpolates between ab initio free-energy points.
Interpolation preserves the critical free-energy contributions from vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
Transferring learned behavior to uncharted regions reduces the need for extensive AIMD runs across phases and compositions.
The ML-assisted free-energy predictions will be within 5–10% of explicit AIMD results.
The method will be at least ten times faster than TOR-TILD and full ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The approach is expected to be valid when adequately representative ab initio training data can be generated.
Early elemental and binary results support the ability of ML potentials to interpolate free-energy landscapes.
Accuracy in extreme composition spaces or at temperatures significantly removed from melting is uncertain.
Transferability to highly complex multicomponent systems and the error across the fusion transition require quantitative benchmarking.
Deviation greater than approximately 10% in free-energy curves or derived fusion properties, or a speedup below tenfold, will falsify the hypothesis.
